timeline.message:
Efficient BytBuf search algorithms (#9914)

Motivation:

We have found out that ByteBufUtil.indexOf can be inefficient for substring search on
ByteBuf, both in terms of algorithm complexity (worst case O(needle.readableBytes *
haystack.readableBytes)), and in constant factor (esp. on Composite buffers).
With implementation of more performant search algorithms we have seen improvements on
the order of magnitude.

Modifications:

This change introduces three search algorithms:
1. Knuth Morris Pratt - classical textbook algorithm, a good default choice.
2. Bit mask based algorithm - stable performance on any input, but limited to maximum
search substring (the needle) length of 64 bytes.
3. Aho–Corasick - worse performance and higher memory consumption than [1] and [2], but
it supports multiple substring (the needles) search simultaneously, by inspecting every
byte of the haystack only once.

Each algorithm processes every byte of underlying buffer only once, they are implemented
as ByteProcessor.

Result:

Efficient search algorithms with linear time complexity available in Netty (I will share
benchmark results in a comment on a PR).

timeline.body:
Motivation:

We have found out that `ByteBufUtil.indexOf` can be inefficient for substring search on
`ByteBuf`, both in terms of algorithm complexity (worst case `O(needle.readableBytes *
haystack.readableBytes)`), and in constant factor (esp. on Composite buffers).
With implementation of more performant search algorithms we have seen improvements on
the order of magnitude.

Modifications:

This change introduces three search algorithms:
1. [Knuth Morris Pratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knuth–Morris–Pratt_algorithm) - classical textbook algorithm, a good default choice.
2. Bit mask based algorithm - stable performance on any input, but limited to maximum
search substring (the `needle`) length of 64 bytes.
3. [Aho–Corasick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aho–Corasick_algorithm) - worse performance and higher memory consumption than [1] and [2], but it supports multiple substring (the `needles`) 
search simultaneously, by inspecting every byte of the `haystack` only once.

Each algorithm processes every byte of underlying buffer only once, they are implemented
as `ByteProcessor`.

Result:

Efficient search algorithms with linear time complexity available in Netty (I will share
benchmark results in a comment on a PR).

Fixes #9914.

Thanks for pushing me in the right direction, @franz1981 . Even though the patterns here look quite different from the ones in #9942, I've realised that one of my benchmark inputs was too flawed - the first byte of the `needle` was never present in the `haystack`, and this made `Kntuh-Morris-Pratt` and `ByteBufUtil.indexOf` runs absolutely predictable, giving them some unfair advantage (the other two search algos are effectively branch free). I've dropped the flawed input and added two randomized `haystacks` (256 and 2048 bytes long). 

Also, added a case with `directBuffer` to help `ByteBufUtil.indexOf` take advantage of `getLong` based traversal in `equals` (BTW, some additional tests showed that this optimization of `ByteBufUtil.equals` backfires on heap based buffers, likely because it has to boil down to 8 `getByte` accesses, but that is offtopic for this PR).

timeline.body:
Added two more benchmark inputs:
`PREDICTABLE` - the first byte of the `needle` is absent from the `haystack`, triggering fixed branch decisions (this is the perfect case for branch sensitive implementations)
`UNPREDICTABLE` - both `needle` and `haystack` are random sequences of `1`s and `0`s, triggering random branching

As I would expect, there is substantial difference between these two inputs for branch sensitive implementations (`Knuth-Morris-Pratt` and `ByteBufUtil.indexOf`), and no effect at all for branch-free algorithms (`Shifting Bit Mask` and `Aho-Corasic`).

`PREDICTABLE` is the only input on which `kmp` is the fastest, with `shiftingBitMask` falling behind it.

The challenge with these benchmarks is that there are multiple dimensions of input sizes and contents, affecting different implementations in different ways. Because of that, I have suggested somewhere in the Javadocs that benchmarking based on concrete use cases should be performed for selecting an optimal algorithm for that particular case.

@franz1981 if you would like to see the results for some particular inputs, please be more specific.

Also, I'm really interested in seeing branch predictor results to verify my assumptions, but this seems unattainable on OSX / DTraceAsm (I'd be happy to hear that I'm wrong), and will take me some additional time to do.

Benchmarking search methods is complex, that's for sure! And trying to trick the branch predictor while doing it, even more: I still think that a "different" benchmark could try to mimic some more realistic usage of these search algos like:

- searching for the same needle in the same trial, but without GC involved
- iterating trough different-sized and *many* haystacks on each `@Benchmark`, while preserving the same expected behaviour for the algorithm eg worst case but using different permutations of the haystack bytes

And maybe it could finally trick the branch predictor while preserving numbers that could be used for some real use case (hopefully!).
I've no idea if it's some realistic task for this, but my concern is due to your comment on
> but I find their absolute numbers (that are in single or low double digits) surprisingly low. Could it be that speculative execution gets turned off for unpredictable branch and no more misses get accounted for (that's just a wild speculation, didn't find anything like that on the web, but I have no other ideas)?

That seems perfectly plausible to me.

In addition ByteBuf boundchecks could be disabled/enabled to allow easier comparisons.

When benchmarking tight loops on Intel CPUs please make sure that you have microcode before JCC Erratum or you've used some options which align jumps in 32-byte boundary like [here](https://github.com/oracle/graal/issues/1829).

I have some good progress planned for the next few days (a tangible performance improvement, a new structure for benchmarks). I think after that your suggestion might be worth considering.

I could be wrong, but: what happen if the remaining bytes to search in are less then the needle to search for?
The original quadratic Netty algo was failing immediately, while now I'm not sure is happening, probably due to the `BytesProcessor` abstraction.
It's interesting to see that many KMP implementation around on internet (including wikipedia) are just ignoring to fail fast (or faster) :)

In addition, re the KMP algorithm: 

- the algo can be modified by using a null jump table if it contains just 0s: due to how final work, the JVM will null check it anyway, so better to use it at our advantage, treating that case like a 0-valued jump: this would save any array access
- the jump table could be made shorter of 1 element because the first element is always 0 (not a big deal)

> I could be wrong, but: what happen if the remaining bytes to search in are less then the needle to search for?
> The original quadratic Netty algo was failing immediately, while now I'm not sure is happening, probably due to the `BytesProcessor` abstraction.

You are right, @franz1981 . `BytesProcessor` based implementations cannot take advantage of this knowledge because they are not aware of remaining `haystack` length.
~This could be solved at higher level by using `ByteBuf.forEachByte(int index, int length, ByteProcessor processor)` instead of `forEachByte(ByteProcessor processor)`.~ (edit - see the comment below)

FYI, for the reason that you mention, the very worst case for quadratic algorithm is when the `haystack` is 2 times longer than the `needle`.

@linasm 

> Not very useful IMHO. This callback based API is not well suited for such optimization.

Agree :( 
Anyway it's a shame that although `ByteBuf::forEach` is aware of the remaining bytes to be processed (it uses start/end) the processor cannot stop earlier...

Re my other comment about using a null jump table I still think it worths to be done (or benchmarks will prove me I'm wrong, that often happen :D )

    + Netty 4.1.45.Final released +

    +

    + + by + normanmaurer +
    + on + 13-Jan-2020 +     +

    +
    +

    I am happy to announce the release of netty 4.1.45.Final, our first release of 2020. This is a bug-fix release which also fixes two regressions. Please upgrade as soon as possible.

    +

    For more details please read-on.

    +

    The most important changes in this release are:

    +
      +
    • Fix BufferOverflowException during non-Unsafe PooledDirectByteBuf resize (#9912)
      • +
    • FlushConsolidationHandler may suppress flushes by mistake (#9931)
      • +
    • Utf8FrameValidator must release buffer when validation fails (#9909)
      • +
    • Avoid possible comparison contract violation (#9883)
      • +
    • Ignore inline comments when parsing nameservers (#9894)
      • +
    +

    For the details and all changes, please browse our issue tracker for 4.1.45.Final.

    +

    Thank You

    +

For more details please read-on.

+

The most important changes in this release are:

+

    • +

For the details and all changes, please browse our issue tracker for 4.1.45.Final.

Implemented a new benchmark suite [`SearchRealDataBenchmark`](https://github.com/netty/netty/pull/9955/files#diff-e458d32e84d03c06cea6f99224ea4da2). It is using a 15 KB html file taken from https://netty.io/news/2020/01/13/4-1-45-Final.html as a haystack.
Also, a mix of 10 needles with varying frequency of occurrence within the haystack.
There are 3 benchmarks:
- `findFirst` - searches the haystack from the beginning to the first occurrence of the needle
- `findFirstFromIndex` - same as `findFirst`, but starts the search from some varying position
- `findAll` - iterates the whole haystack, finding every occurrence of the needle

@franz1981 is this move in the direction you had in your mind?

Results (here I am reusing a unique search processor for each needle, resetting its internal state between benchmark invocations, which I believe has disadvantages I will describe in the next comment):

In the results above, I was reusing a unique `SearchProcessor` per each `needle`, by resetting its internal state between invocations. This makes the `SearchProcessor` escape the method scope, slowing down the execution (because internal state gets updated on the object field with reuse; without reuse the internal state is contained in a CPU register).
I believe in practice a new `SearchProcessor` should be allocated per each case of searching for the same needle. It is very cheap object (3 fields in case of all algorithms; their values are simply set during construction, without any additional logics), and benchmarks show this approach to be more performant.
Results of the new benchmark suite, with no reuse of `SearchProcessor`:

Yep and I agree that, given that the `jumpTable` is reused without being created each time, the GC pressure should be low enough to be ignored, but still i suggest to run the benchmarks with `prof gc` and with some miss branches profiling on to see the effect of GC and if now the misses are what we expect them to be :+1:

@franz1981 `-prof gc` shows that allocations / GC is basically non-exeistent for all 3 algorithms on all benchmark/buffer type combinations, such as:
```

```

```

```
So when `SearchProcessor` is not escaping, the compiler is doing great job of scalar replacing its fields on stack (or on CPU registers, like assembly code shows).

Regarding branch CPU counters, again sadly it will take me a while getting them (wrong OS...).

Have CPU counter results (below) for the new benchmark suite. 
Sharing full results here: https://gist.github.com/linasm/aef06520f3fa63c00ec1602acc55876f

Some observations:
- branch misses in "branch-free" algorithms (`AHO_CORASIC`, `SHIFTING_BIT_MASK`) are negligible
- in `KMP` they are higher by up to 2 orders of magnitude
- `AHO_CORASIC` suffers from high CPI (0.6) which cannot be explained by other counters (such as branch or cache misses which are very low) so I would try to explain by it's recursive memory access pattern performed in a tight loop, causing pipeline stalls

These are all the insights based on my very limited experience with CPU performance counters.
